name: Cista++
workload: Serialize/deserialize/traverse a graph-shaped data structure (nodes+edges) using Google Benchmark, comparing Cista++ (offset & raw modes) against Cap'n Proto, cereal, and FlatBuffers.
claimed_speedup: ~1.12-1.14x faster traverse and deserialize+traverse than FlatBuffers (67ms/66ms vs 75ms/75ms); 2.5x smaller serialized size (25.3MB vs 63.0MB) in offset mode (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11, CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (exact optimization flags beyond Release not itemized)
tradeoffs: No cross-language schema evolution like Protobuf/Cap'n Proto; reader/writer must share pointer width; only C++17 can read/write today; raw mode requires larger buffers than offset mode
caveats: The same benchmark table also shows raw serialize (4ms vs 1409ms) and deserialize (0.16ms vs 35.7ms) numbers implying a 200-350x gap; this looks like an artifact of how the FlatBuffers builder constructs many small nested offsets for this specific graph shape rather than a representative workload, so those extreme ratios were excluded from the headline claim. Benchmark authored by the Cista maintainer, not independently audited.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:serialization language:C++ --sort stars, then opened felixguendling/cista README and its linked benchmark repo

name: zpp_bits (evidence update)
workload: Same graph serialize/deserialize/traverse benchmark as the Cista++ entry (nodes+edges, Google Benchmark), comparing zpp_bits against Cap'n Proto, cereal, Cista++, and FlatBuffers.
claimed_speedup: ~5.4x faster deserialize than FlatBuffers (6.58ms vs 35.7ms) and ~1.15x faster traverse (65ms vs 75ms); 1.7x smaller serialized size (37.8MB vs 63.0MB) (derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++20-only; no cross-language codegen like FlatBuffers/Protobuf
caveats: Same benchmark also shows a raw serialize number (4ms vs FlatBuffers 1409ms, ~350x) that looks implausible for the reasons noted in the Cista++ entry and was excluded from the headline claim. zpp_bits is already on the known-list; this is new Tier A third-party-repo evidence (independent of zpp_bits' own author) found while researching this category, hence is_evidence_for_known=true.
found_via: GitHub: opened felixguendling/cpp-serialization-benchmark README while evaluating Cista++

name: Bitsery
workload: Serialize/deserialize a ~10KB nested domain object (Monster: vec3, strings, vectors, nested structs) repeatedly (300,000 samples), comparing bitsery, boost, cereal, flatbuffers, msgpack, protobuf, yas, and zpp_bits.
claimed_speedup: ~19x faster serialize (1119ms vs 21229ms) and ~19x faster deserialize (1166ms vs 22077ms) than Protobuf, with a smaller wire size (6913B vs 10018B)
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11 / Clang 12.0.1, CMake Release build (exact optimization flags not itemized)
hardware: Ubuntu 20.04 x64 (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: No IDL/schema generator; user writes a serialize() function per type; forward/backward compatibility is opt-in via an extension rather than built-in like Protobuf
caveats: Benchmark repo is authored by bitsery's own maintainer (first-party); CPU model not disclosed, only OS/arch, so it falls short of Tier A despite public code and stated compilers.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:serialization language:C++ --sort stars, then opened fraillt/bitsery README and linked benchmark repo

name: YAS (Yet Another Serialization)
workload: Serialize+deserialize a moderately sized object (two arrays: numbers and strings) 1,000,000 times, averaged over 50 runs, comparing thrift, protobuf, boost, msgpack, cereal, avro, and yas.
claimed_speedup: ~7.6x faster than Protobuf (302.7ms vs 2312.78ms avg. total time for 1M serialize+deserialize ops); smaller compact output (yas-compact 13,321B vs protobuf 16,116B)
compiler_and_flags: cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release; project says it was tested with Clang and GCC but does not state which compiler produced the published numbers
hardware: "Intel Core i7 processor", Ubuntu 16.04 (exact CPU model/generation not given)
tradeoffs: No IDL/schema, no built-in forward/backward compatibility (listed as a TODO); header-only and boost-free, but far less tooling than protobuf
caveats: Benchmark dataset is old (protobuf 3.7.0, thrift 0.12.0, from ~2019); the yas repository itself has no LICENSE file, so it is not clearly OSI-licensed (treated as reference-only, study-not-copy).
found_via: GitHub: cross-referenced via the 'Other Benchmarks' links in felixguendling/cpp-serialization-benchmark and the bitsery README, then opened thekvs/cpp-serializers and niXman/yas

name: YaFF (Yet another Flat Format)
workload: Median time to read every field out of an already-serialized buffer, for flat messages (10/100 uint64 fields) and a 3-level hierarchical message under hot (~2KB working set) and cold (~512MB working set) access patterns, using google/benchmark.
claimed_speedup: Flat Layout reads are ~25-50x faster than Protobuf and ~2-2.5x faster than FlatBuffers on flat messages (e.g. 100-field flat read: 25.99ns YaFF vs 1383.74ns Protobuf vs 54.81ns FlatBuffers); hierarchical hot access is ~25x faster than Protobuf and ~3.5x faster than FlatBuffers
compiler_and_flags: Clang 20.1.8, Release build, benchmarks built with google/benchmark
tradeoffs: Still requires an existing .proto schema (built as a companion physical layout for Protobuf, not a schema replacement); adds adaptive-layout complexity; C++ only today, multi-language bindings are roadmap items
caveats: Very young project under active development; benchmark is first-party but methodology, exact hardware, and compiler are fully disclosed (meets the Tier A bar); authors note absolute numbers depend on the EPYC 7713's DDR4 memory subsystem, though they claim the relative ratios generalize.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:flatbuffers --sort stars, then opened yandex/yaff README and docs/benchmarks

name: ProtoCache
workload: Decode+traverse+deallocate (and reflection-based decode+traverse) of a Protobuf-schema message, plus full serialization of the complex twitter.proto dataset, comparing Protobuf, ProtoCache, ProtoCacheEX, FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto, and Fory.
claimed_speedup: ~20x faster decode+traverse+dealloc than Protobuf (132ns vs 2620ns); ~30x faster with reflection (270ns vs 8189ns); ProtoCacheEX serializes twitter.proto ~2.1x faster than Protobuf (101us vs 215us)
benchmark_url: https://github.com/PeterRK/protocache (README.md benchmark tables; code in test/benchmark)
tradeoffs: Requires an existing Protobuf schema/toolchain (protoc + protoc-gen-pccx plugin); ProtoCache's own plain Serialize is actually slower than Protobuf per its own table (6493ns vs 557ns) — the win is specifically on decode/traverse, not on encode
caveats: No CPU model, compiler, or compiler flags disclosed for the timing benchmark, only that it is a Release-ish native-optimized build; small project (83 stars); numbers are first-party.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:flatbuffers --sort stars, then opened PeterRK/protocache README

name: Simple Binary Encoding (SBE)
workload: Serialize/deserialize a small trading domain object (Account + Wallet + 3 Orders, ~120-280 bytes on the wire) via chronoxor's CppBenchmark-based CppSerialization suite, comparing Cap'n Proto, FastBinaryEncoding, FlatBuffers, Protobuf, SBE, zpp::bits, and JSON.
claimed_speedup: ~9.2x faster serialize (35ns vs 322ns) and ~6.75x faster deserialize (52ns vs 351ns) than Protobuf
compiler_and_flags: CppBenchmark harness, "Process configuration: release"; exact compiler name/version used for the published table is not stated (repo's own CI covers GCC, Clang and MSVC)
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, 10 cores (10 physical), 2.4GHz, macOS 24.5.0 (one of several per-run hardware configs logged in the repo)
tradeoffs: Requires an SBE XML schema and code generator; designed around FIX-derived low-latency financial messaging, less flexible than Protobuf for evolving/optional fields
caveats: Benchmark run by a third party (chronoxor, unaffiliated with SBE's aeron-io maintainers) rather than SBE's own team, which makes this a reasonably independent Tier-B source; the message under test is tiny and fixed-size, so results may not generalize to larger/variable-length messages.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:flatbuffers --sort stars surfaced chronoxor/CppSerialization, which benchmarks SBE against Protobuf

name: Fast Binary Encoding (FBE)
workload: Same Account/Wallet/Orders domain-object serialize/deserialize benchmark as the SBE entry, using chronoxor's own CppBenchmark-based CppSerialization suite.
claimed_speedup: ~9.5x faster serialize (66ns vs 628ns) and ~9.3x faster deserialize (82ns vs 759ns) than Protobuf
compiler_and_flags: CppBenchmark harness, release configuration; exact compiler unspecified in the summary table
hardware: Not stated in the summary table (per-run detailed reports elsewhere in the repo show configurations such as Apple M1 Pro)
tradeoffs: Requires its own FBE schema/IDL and code generator; C++ is the reference implementation, other language ports may lag in performance
caveats: First-party benchmark: FastBinaryEncoding and the comparison repo (CppSerialization) share the same author (chronoxor). Numbers vary slightly between runs in the repo's own history (e.g. one run shows 77ns/84ns, another 66ns/82ns), suggesting normal measurement noise rather than an issue with the library.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:serialization language:C++ --sort stars, then opened chronoxor/FastBinaryEncoding README

name: Apache Fory (C++)
workload: Serialize/deserialize three C++ structs of increasing complexity (NumericStruct, Sample, MediaContent) using Google Benchmark, comparing Fory's C++ implementation against Protobuf.
claimed_speedup: 1.2x-4.5x higher throughput than Protobuf across cases: MediaContent serialize 4.5x (2,254,915 vs 504,410 ops/sec), MediaContent deserialize 1.9x, Sample serialize/deserialize ~1.3x, NumericStruct serialize 1.6x / deserialize 1.2x
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build, C++17 (repo states GCC 8+/Clang 7+/MSVC 2019+ are supported); exact compiler/version used for the published numbers is not stated
hardware: Darwin 24.5.0, arm64, 12 physical/12 logical cores, 48GB RAM (specific CPU model, e.g. which Apple silicon chip, not named)
tradeoffs: Much larger, multi-language xlang framework rather than a lightweight C++-only library; C++ support is newer and less battle-tested than Fory's Java implementation
caveats: First-party benchmark (Apache Fory's own repo); exact CPU model and compiler version not disclosed; C++ gains (1.2-4.5x) are more modest than several other zero-copy competitors in this list, unlike Fory's much larger claimed Java-only wins (up to 170x vs JDK serialization, a different comparison not against Protobuf).
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/apache/fory metadata lookup after seeing Fory referenced as a comparison target in PeterRK/protocache's README, then opened apache/fory README and benchmarks/cpp
